{{Short description|Field in materials science and mechanics}}
'''Poroelasticity''' is a field in [[materials science]] and mechanics that studies the interaction between fluid flow, pressure and bulk solid deformation within a linear [[porous medium]] and it is an extension of elasticity and porous medium flow ([[diffusion equation]]). The deformation of the medium influences the flow of the fluid and vice versa. The theory was proposed by [[Maurice Anthony Biot]] (1935, 1941)<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Biot|first=Maurice A. | name-list-style = vanc |date=1941-02-01|title=General Theory of Three‐Dimensional Consolidation|journal=Journal of Applied Physics|volume=12|issue=2|pages=155–164|doi=10.1063/1.1712886|bibcode=1941JAP....12..155B |issn=0021-8979|url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-01368635/document }}</ref> as a theoretical extension of [[soil consolidation]] models developed to calculate the settlement of structures placed on fluid-saturated porous soils.
The theory of poroelasticity has been widely applied in [[geomechanics]],<ref name="Cheng_2016">{{cite book | title = Poroelasticity | volume = 27 | publisher = Springer | last = Cheng | first = Alexander H.-D.| name-list-style = vanc | doi = 10.1007/978-3-319-25202-5 | year = 2016| series = Theory and Applications of Transport in Porous Media | isbn = 978-3-319-25200-1 | s2cid = 240649873 mechanics,<ref>{{Citation|last1=Malandrino|first1=Andrea|title=Poroelasticity of Living Tissues|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B978012801238399932X|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of An intuitive sense of the response of a saturated elastic porous medium to mechanical loading can be developed by thinking about, or experimenting with, a fluid-saturated sponge. If a fluid- saturated sponge is compressed, fluid will flow from the sponge. If the sponge is in a fluid reservoir and compressive pressure is subsequently removed, the sponge will reimbibe the fluid and expand. The volume of the sponge will also increase if its exterior openings are sealed and the pore fluid pressure is increased. The basic ideas underlying the theory of poroelastic materials are that the pore fluid pressure contributes to the total stress in the porous matrix medium and that the pore fluid pressure alone can strain the porous matrix medium. There is fluid movement in a porous medium due to differences in pore fluid pressure created by different pore volume strains associated with mechanical loading of the porous medium.<ref name="Tissue Mechanics - Springer">{{cite book|title=Tissue Mechanics|publisher=Springer|year=2007|isbn=978-0-387-36825-2|editor-last1=Cowin|editor-first1=Stephen C.|doi=10.1007/978-0-387-49985-7|editor-last2=Doty|editor-first2=Stephen B.|name-list-style=vanc}}</ref> In [[Unconventional (oil & gas) reservoir|unconventional reservoir]] and source rocks for natural gas like coal and shales, there can be strain due to sorption of gases like methane and [[carbon dioxide]] on the porous rock surfaces.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Zoback|first1=Mark D.|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/unconventional-reservoir-geomechanics/39665444034A2EF143D749DF48A5E5DC|title=Unconventional Reservoir Geomechanics: Shale Gas, Tight Oil, and Induced Seismicity|last2=Kohli|first2=Arjun H.|date=2019|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-107-08707-1|location=Cambridge|doi=10.1017/9781316091869|s2cid=197568886}}</ref> Depending on the gas pressure the induced sorption-based strain can be poroelastic or poroinelastic in nature.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Saurabh|first1=Suman|last2=Harpalani|first2=Satya|date=2018-01-01|title=The effective stress law for stress-sensitive transversely isotropic rocks|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1365160917303738|journal=International Journal of Rock Mechanics and Mining Sciences|language=en|volume=101|pages=69–77|doi=10.1016/j.ijrmms.2017.11.015|issn=1365-1609|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Types of Poroelasticity ==
The theories of poroelasticity can be divided into two categories: static (or quasi-static) and dynamic theories,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.multiphysics.us/poroelasticity.html|title=Multiphysics - Poroelasticity and Poromechanics|last=Liu|first=Zhen (Leo)|website=www.multiphysics.us|access-date=2018-10-03}}</ref> just like mechanics can be divided into statics and dynamics. The static poroelasticity considers processes in which the fluid movement and solid skeleton deformation occur simultaneously and affect each other. The static poroelasticity is predominant in the literature for poroelasticity; as a result, this term is used interchangeably with poroelasticity in many publications. This static poroelasticity theory is a generalization of the one-dimensional consolidation theory in [[soil mechanics]]. This theory was developed from Biot's work in 1941.<ref name=":0" /> The dynamic poroelasticity is proposed for understanding the wave propagation in both the liquid and solid phases of saturated porous materials. The inertial and associated [[kinetic energy]], which are not considered in static poroelasticity, are included. This is especially necessary when the speed of the movement of the phases in the porous material is considerable, e.g., when vibration or stress waves is present.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|url=https://www.springer.com/us/book/9783319930275|title=Multiphysics in Porous Materials |author = Zhen (Leo) Liu |language=en|isbn=9783319930275|publisher=Springer|year=2018}}</ref> The dynamic poroelasticity was developed attributed to Biot's work on the propagation of elastic waves in fluid-saturated media.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Biot|first=M. A.|date=April 1962|title=Mechanics of Deformation and Acoustic Propagation in Porous Media|journal=Journal of Applied Physics|language=en|volume=33|issue=4|pages=1482–1498|doi=10.1063/1.1728759|bibcode=1962JAP....33.1482B|s2cid=58914453 |issn=0021-8979|url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-01368725/file/Mechanics%20of%20deformation%20and%20acoustic%20propagation%20in%20porous%20media.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Biot|first=M. A.|date=March 1956|title=Theory of Propagation of Elastic Waves in a Fluid‐Saturated Porous Solid. II. Higher Frequency Range|journal=The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America|language=en|volume=28|issue=2|pages=179–191|doi=10.1121/1.1908241|bibcode=1956ASAJ...28..179B|issn=0001-4966|url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-01368668/file/Theory%20of%20propagation%20of%20elastic%20waves%20in%20a%20fluid%E2%80%90saturated%20porous%20solid.%20II.%20Higher%20frequency%20range.pdf}}</ref>

== Laboratory Measurements ==
Three type of tests are commonly used to determine the poroelastic parameters:<ref name=":2">{{Citation |last=Detournay |first=E. |chapter=Fundamentals of Poroelasticity |date=1993 |title=Analysis and Design Methods |pages=113–171 |chapter-url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/B9780080406152500113 |access-date=2026-03-16 |publisher=Elsevier |language=en |doi=10.1016/b978-0-08-040615-2.50011-3 |isbn=978-0-08-040615-2 |last2=Cheng |first2=Alexander H.-D.|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Drained test ===
In a drained test, the confining pressure is increased while the pore pressure at the boundary of the material is kept at its initial value. Consequently, an incremental pore pressure is initially generated within the rock, corresponding to an undrained condition. This excess pore pressure gradually dissipates as the system equilibrates with the imposed boundary pore pressure. From this test, two measurements can be obtained: the volume change of the material and the volume of fluid removed from the material.<ref name=":2" />

=== Undrained test ===
In an undrained test, similar to a drained test, the confining pressure applied to the material is increased. However, the key difference is that no fluid is allowed to leave the sample during the test. Under this condition, the increase in confining pressure induces a change in pore pressure within the material. This test allows the measurement of the volumetric change of the sample and the corresponding change in pore pressure.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wissa |first=Anwar E. Z. |date=July 1969 |title=Pore Pressure Measurement in Saturated Stiff Soils |url=https://doi.org/10.1061/jsfeaq.0001304 |journal=Journal of the Soil Mechanics and Foundations Division |volume=95 |issue=4 |pages=1063–1073 |doi=10.1061/jsfeaq.0001304 |issn=0044-7994|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Unjacketed test ===
Unlike the previous two tests, no controlled confining pressure is applied directly to the sample. Instead, the sample is placed in a pressure vessel, where equal increments of confining pressure and pore pressure are applied simultaneously. Since the pore pressure varies during the test, calibration is required to determine the change in fluid volume within the sample. This test enables the measurement of the unjacketed compressibility and a storage coefficient defined under equal-pressure loading conditions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Biot |first=M. A. |last2=Willis |first2=D. G. |date=1957-12-01 |title=The Elastic Coefficients of the Theory of Consolidation |url=https://doi.org/10.1115/1.4011606 |journal=Journal of Applied Mechanics |volume=24 |issue=4 |pages=594–601 |doi=10.1115/1.4011606 |issn=0021-8936|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
